newsitem.title: USA: U.S. spot natgas prices slip in East, rise in West.
newsitem.headline: U.S. spot natgas prices slip in East, rise in West.

text.p: U.S. spot natgas prices, influenced by differing weather patterns, were weaker in the Midwest and Gulf markets but stronger in the western markets, industry sources said Friday.
Gulf Coast prices fell an average of five cents to the low-to-mid $2.40s in volatile trading, with late deals reported done in the mid-to-high $2.40s.
Some sources attributed the rise in Gulf cash to the higher-than-expected opening of NYMEX's expiring November Henry Hub contract in the high-$2.40s to low-$2.50s.
In south Texas, seasonable weather patterns pushed prices into the mid-$2.30s despite Texas Eastern's scheduled maintenance in the area, which is expected to be complete Tuesday.
In the Midcontinent, prices fell early into the mid-to-high $2.20s, but some late shortcovering boosted prices into the low-to-mid $2.30s as some cold weather spurts lingered in parts of the region.
As supply remained tight in the western U.S. and Canada, Permian prices gained about five cents to the mid-to-high $2.30s.
Sources noted the shortage of electricity in California and the sustained strong demand in Canada also boosted southern California border prices.

Bonneville Power Administration reported earlier today it offered no surplus power for the weekend and limited Monday sales to 300 megawatts during peak demand hours. In addition, BPA raised prices for Monday peak delivery by $2.00 per megawatt hour.
Traders reported closing most deals at the California border in the high-$2.50s for the weekend, up about 10 cents from Thursday's level.
Similarly in the San Juan basin, prices remained strong in the $2.30s.
In contrast, prices at the New York city-gate fell as low as the $2.60 area because of turned-back gas for the weekend. However, a late scramble for gas pushed prices as high as $2.80.
